00:00:05.000 --> 00:00:08.000 line:65%
Thanks, Professor Skye. Hey everyone, I'm

00:00:08.000 --> 00:00:10.000 line:65%
Lizzie and I'm Viren and we work at Google

00:00:10.000 --> 00:00:12.000 line:65%
Research creating detailed maps of the

00:00:12.000 --> 00:00:14.000 line:65%
brain's wiring to better understand how

00:00:14.000 --> 00:00:15.000 line:65%
brains work.

00:00:15.000 --> 00:00:17.000
One of the coolest things about this

00:00:17.000 --> 00:00:19.000
project is that we're using AI to help

00:00:19.000 --> 00:00:22.000
us decipher the mysteries of the brain,

00:00:22.000 --> 00:00:23.000
which is still one of the biggest

00:00:23.000 --> 00:00:25.000
unanswered questions in science.

00:00:25.000 --> 00:00:27.000
Here's how we're doing it. We start with

00:00:27.000 --> 00:00:29.000
tiny pieces of brain tissue far thinner

00:00:29.000 --> 00:00:30.000
than a human hair. Using a special

00:00:30.000 --> 00:00:32.000
microscope, we capture thousands of

00:00:32.000 --> 00:00:35.000
pictures of these slices. We then

00:00:35.000 --> 00:00:36.000
outline the cells on each slice and

00:00:36.000 --> 00:00:38.000
combine them to create a

00:00:38.000 --> 00:00:40.000
three-dimensional view of a small part

00:00:40.000 --> 00:00:41.000
of the brain.

00:00:41.000 --> 00:00:43.000
In the past, scientists would do this

00:00:43.000 --> 00:00:45.000
all by hand, which was an incredibly

00:00:45.000 --> 00:00:48.000
slow process. For example, it took 16

00:00:48.000 --> 00:00:50.000
years to map the tiny brain of a worm.

00:00:50.000 --> 00:00:52.000
This is where AI comes in. Just like you

00:00:52.000 --> 00:00:54.000
experienced on the quest, we train an AI

00:00:54.000 --> 00:00:56.000
model to look at these pictures and

00:00:56.000 --> 00:00:58.000
trace the tiny and intricate paths of

00:00:58.000 --> 00:01:00.000
each cell. This is an incredibly complex

00:01:00.000 --> 00:01:01.000
task because of a single brain cell

00:01:01.000 --> 00:01:03.000
which can have thousands of connections

00:01:03.000 --> 00:01:05.000
and they're all tangled up like a bowl

00:01:05.000 --> 00:01:07.000
of spaghetti. In this process, we are

00:01:07.000 --> 00:01:09.000
segmenting or separating the individual

00:01:09.000 --> 00:01:11.000
cells from the rest of the tissue. We

00:01:11.000 --> 00:01:12.000
also have to identify the synapses,

00:01:12.000 --> 00:01:14.000
which are the tiny connections where

00:01:14.000 --> 00:01:15.000
different cells pass signals to one

00:01:16.000 --> 00:01:18.000 line:75%
another. Once the AI model has traced

00:01:18.000 --> 00:01:20.000 line:75%
all the cells and identified the

00:01:20.000 --> 00:01:22.000 line:75%
synapses, we can create a complete map

00:01:22.000 --> 00:01:25.000 line:75%
of all of the connections in that part

00:01:25.000 --> 00:01:27.000 line:75%
of the brain. This map is called the

00:01:27.000 --> 00:01:28.000 line:75%
connectome.

00:01:28.000 --> 00:01:30.000 line:95%
Right now, scientists are working on a

00:01:30.000 --> 00:01:32.000 line:95%
connectome of a mouse brain. But our

00:01:32.000 --> 00:01:34.000 line:95%
ultimate goal is to one day map the

00:01:34.000 --> 00:01:35.000 line:95%
human brain. This could help us better

00:01:35.000 --> 00:01:37.000
understand and treat brain-related

00:01:37.000 --> 00:01:38.000
health challenges.

00:01:38.000 --> 00:01:40.000
This incredible journey is an example of

00:01:40.000 --> 00:01:43.000
how AI can turbocharge scientists. It's

00:01:43.000 --> 00:01:44.000
helping us do something that would be

00:01:44.000 --> 00:01:46.000
impossible for scientists to do alone.

00:01:46.000 --> 00:01:49.000
And this quest demonstrates how AI can

00:01:49.000 --> 00:01:51.000
help us unlock the secrets of the brain,

00:01:51.000 --> 00:01:52.000
one cell at a time.

00:01:52.000 --> 00:01:54.000
Be sure to try out our other quests and

00:01:54.000 --> 00:01:56.000
get inspired by impactful work my

00:01:56.000 --> 00:01:57.000
friends at Google Research are doing

00:01:57.000 --> 00:01:59.000
with AI. Back to you, Professor Skye.

tokens.name: The Neuron
tokens.token_collected_dialog: What are neurons? What do they do?

token_info_pages.heading: What are neurons?
token_info_pages.body: {{ Neurons }} are brain cells that send and receive signals. By connecting with other neurons, they allow information to travel through the brain. Your brain has about 86 billion neurons!

token_info_pages.heading: How do neurons communicate?
token_info_pages.body: Tiny gaps between connected neurons are called {{ synapses }} . Chemical signals travel across synapses, carrying messages from one neuron to the next.

tokens.name: Brain
tokens.token_collected_dialog: What is the brain? How does it work?

token_info_pages.heading: What does the brain do?
token_info_pages.body: The {{ brain }} controls thinking, memory, movement, and the senses.  It is also where our memories are formed and stored.

token_info_pages.heading: What is it made of?
token_info_pages.body: Inside the brain, a massive network of cells processes information. These cells are called {{ neurons }} , and memory depends on how they connect to each other.

tokens.name: Microscope
tokens.token_collected_dialog: What does the brain look like on a microscopic scale?

token_info_pages.heading: How small are the samples?
token_info_pages.body: Scientists study brain connections at a {{ microscopic scale. }} They scan thousands of thin brain slices. These slices are 3,000x thinner than a human hair!

token_info_pages.heading: What can scientists see in those images?
token_info_pages.body: The images are detailed enough to show tiny structures in the brain, including neurons and blood vessels.

tokens.name: Professor Axon's Story
tokens.token_collected_dialog: What has Professor Axon been working on? What's his story?

token_info_pages.heading: What’s the professor’s story?
token_info_pages.body:
Professor Axon is a {{ neuroscientist }} who has dedicated his life to studying the brain.
His goal has always been to create a {{ 3D map }} of brain connections related to memory. He has worked on it for decades - and still isn’t close to finishing!

token_info_pages.heading: What is he doing in Polar Peaks?
token_info_pages.body:
Professor Axon moved to Polar Peaks to investigate the locals’ forgetfulness. He believes that mapping brain {{ connections }} involved in memory could help reveal what is going wrong.
But the work is very slow to do by hand. He needs your help to train an {{ AI model }} to speed up the research.

tokens.name: Labelling
tokens.token_collected_dialog: How do scientists manually map the brain's connections?

token_info_pages.heading: What is labelling?
token_info_pages.body: Mapping brain connections by hand is an incredibly slow process.  Scientists must manually examine scans of tiny brain slices to identify and {{ label }} neurons, the brain cells that send and receive signals.

token_info_pages.heading: How does labelling help scientists map the brain?
token_info_pages.body: After labelling the cells in each scan, scientists stack the scans together. This builds a 3D map that shows how the neurons connect to each other.
